title: How to Travel the World Without Jet Lag
claims: Flying east requires a phase advance of the circadian clock, whereas flying west requires a phase delay.

It takes longer to reset the circadian clock after eastward than westward flight, partly because the average free-running period of the human circadian clock is slightly longer than 24 hours, making phase advances harder than phase delays.
Early estimates from real jet travellers are that the circadian clock phase delays 92 minutes per day after westward flights and phase advances 57 minutes per day after eastward flights.

Laboratory studies with a 12-hour shift of the sleep-wake schedule found circadian rhythms shifted 9.6 hours over the first 4 days when phase delaying (2.4 hours per day) and 6.2 hours when phase advancing (1.6 hours per day).

Jet travel plans have been developed assuming phase advances of 1.5 hours per day and phase delays of 2 hours per day, given appropriately timed bright light after landing; these numbers are estimates.
